correctness.rationale: For the ordinary game on GP(10,2), the covered set and next mover are sufficient: a previous move's whole closed neighborhood is covered, so no repeated move can be legal. Every proper set admits a move and each legal move strictly enlarges it. With terminal D=S=0, the exact recurrence is D(U)=1+min S(U∪N[v]) and S(U)=1+max D(U∪N[v]) over legal v. The independent reachable-set DAG run used 11,846 dominated masks and checked all openings and all 760 conditional scores for distinct ordered opening/reply pairs under both conventions. It returned roots (9,8), uniform opening values, and distance-1-through-5 totals (9,8,8,8,9) and (9,9,8,9,9). The shell counts are (3,6,6,3,1); distinct closed neighborhoods have the same cardinality four so all nineteen distinct replies are legal. Hence S's optimal replies are neighbors and the antipode (four), while D's are precisely distance three (six). Frozen replay sources and logs are artifacts/game_dp.cpp, game_dp.py, cpp_output.txt and python_output.txt in the record directory; they were inspected, not executed. Independent replay: /workspace/branches/0a2fa392-a5ad-47f5-a702-3f2fd5f52e46/gp102_game_check.py and companion gp102_game_check_output.txt.

value.rationale: A canonical cubic Platonic graph gives a natural test of the difference between starting conventions. The full distance profile explains which replies are responsible, distinguishing neighbors and the antipode from intermediate distances under one start and singling out only distance three under the other. This exact invariant is usable to benchmark strategies and compare other cubic symmetric graphs; it is not just a recomputed scalar or a claim that the starting disadvantage itself is new.
